question: What is the final result of the normal blood clotting process?
explanation: Think of the clotting cascade as a factory assembly line. It finishes by turning fibrinogen into a solid fibrin mesh that weaves together to hold the clot firmly in place. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h1)

question: How do acquired bleeding problems differ from inherited conditions like hemophilia?

options.A: Acquired disorders develop later in life due to illnesses or deficiencies
options.B: Inherited disorders only show up during major surgery in adulthood
options.C: Inherited disorders can be cured easily with simple vitamin supplements
options.D: Acquired disorders only affect red blood cells instead of platelets

explanation: While inherited conditions are passed down in your genes from birth, acquired disorders pop up later in life because of illness, poor nutrition, or certain medications. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h1)

question: Which organ in the body is the main factory for producing most of our blood clotting factors?
explanation: The liver is a busy chemical plant! It produces almost all the important proteins needed for blood to clot properly. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h2)

question: A patient receives several bags of packed red blood cells after an accident, but no plasma. What clotting complication are they most at risk for?
explanation: If you only pump in red blood cells without replacing plasma, you end up diluting the patient's remaining platelets and clotting factors. This is called dilutive coagulopathy. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h2)

question: Why do patients with Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) end up bleeding severely?

options.A: Blood pressure drops so low that blood can no longer flow through vessels
options.B: The bone marrow completely stops making red blood cells and white cells
options.C: The liver starts destroying all circulating proteins in the blood plasma
options.D: All available platelets and clotting factors are used up by widespread tiny clots

explanation: DIC is a confusing condition where the body goes into overdrive, forming tiny clots everywhere. This uses up all the clotting resources, leaving none behind when a real bleed happens elsewhere. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h3)

question: Which serious medical condition is a very common trigger for acute DIC?
explanation: Severe infections and sepsis release a flood of inflammatory chemicals that accidentally trigger widespread clotting all over the body. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h3)

question: Which vitamin does the liver desperately need to build several key clotting factors?
explanation: Vitamin K is like a vital tool in the liver's workshop. Without it, clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X cannot be built. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h4)

question: How can taking broad-spectrum antibiotics for a long time lead to a bleeding risk?

options.A: By blocking the bone marrow from producing new blood platelets
options.B: By directly dissolving the fibrin mesh at old wound sites
options.C: By destroying normal gut bacteria that help produce vitamin K
options.D: By increasing the speed at which the liver breaks down plasma proteins

explanation: Good bacteria live in our guts and actually help make vitamin K for us. Strong antibiotics wipe out these helpful bacteria, which can lower our vitamin K levels. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h4)

question: What are those tiny, pinpoint reddish-purple spots on the skin caused by minor capillary bleeding called?
explanation: Petechiae are tiny little dots of blood right under the skin surface caused by tiny capillaries leaking. You'll often spot them in assessment questions! [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h5)

question: A patient with severe liver disease looks restless, seems confused, and has a fast heart rate with dropping blood pressure. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Perform a comprehensive assessment for internal bleeding and report changes immediately
options.B: Document the findings in the chart and schedule a routine check for the next morning
options.C: Apply warm compresses to the patient's limbs to improve peripheral circulation
options.D: Encourage the patient to get out of bed and walk around the ward to ease restlessness

explanation: Restlessness, confusion, and dropping vitals are classic red flags! They can mean internal bleeding is happening, which needs urgent action. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h5)

question: Which lab test specifically checks the extrinsic and common pathways of blood clotting?
explanation: PT is the go-to lab test to see how quickly the extrinsic pathway and common pathway are getting the job done. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h6)

question: What does a high D-dimer blood test usually tell the healthcare team?

options.A: The body is actively forming and breaking down blood clots
options.B: The patient has a severe primary iron deficiency anemia
options.C: The bone marrow is producing too many immature white cells
options.D: There is a complete lack of red blood cell production

explanation: A D-dimer is essentially microscopic debris left behind when the body dissolves a clot. If it's high, it means clotting and clot-busting are happening somewhere in the body. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h6)

question: Which blood product is usually given to replace multiple missing clotting factors in a patient with severe liver disease?
explanation: Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) is packed with all the liquid plasma proteins and clotting factors a failing liver can no longer make on its own. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h7)

question: Why is treating the root cause just as important as giving blood products when managing DIC?

options.A: The patient's kidneys will immediately filter out all infused platelets if they have a fever
options.B: The body will keep consuming clotting factors as long as the primary trigger remains active
options.C: Blood products will not work unless the patient's room temperature is carefully controlled
options.D: Transfusions can cause permanent damage to the liver if the infection is not cured first

explanation: Think of it like trying to bail water out of a leaking boat without fixing the hole. If you don't stop the infection or trauma causing the DIC, the body will just burn through your new blood products instantly. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h7)

question: A patient with a bleeding disorder needs a blood sample drawn. As a nurse, what is your best action?

options.A: Apply prolonged direct pressure to the venipuncture site after removing the needle
options.B: Massage the puncture site vigorously immediately after pulling out the needle
options.C: Apply a cold ice pack to the arm for thirty minutes before attempting the draw
options.D: Use the largest gauge needle available to speed up the blood collection process

explanation: Because their blood takes longer to form a plug, holding firm, direct pressure on the needle site for an extra-long time prevents large, painful bruises (hematomas). [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h8)

question: Why do nurses always warn patients with bleeding problems to stay away from everyday painkillers like ibuprofen?

options.A: NSAIDs increase blood pressure to dangerous levels and trigger acute strokes
options.B: NSAIDs instantly destroy all stored vitamin K reserves located inside the liver
options.C: NSAIDs negatively interfere with normal platelet aggregation and increase bleeding risks
options.D: NSAIDs cause the kidneys to stop producing red blood cells permanently

explanation: Medications like ibuprofen and aspirin get in the way of platelets sticking together, making it much harder for your body to stop any bleeding. [learn more](GNS311_U2_T11#GNS311_U2_T11_h8)
